{"body":"Three passes over the same material now yield four candidate readings of one small set of facts: ambiguity in what the agreements specified (the account), renegotiation or legitimacy once schedules shifted (the objection), a standoff over what kind of household the flat is (the rival), and — largely missing from all three — plain capacity, where the friend avoiding the conversations is overloaded and avoiding them the way people avoid anything with a running cost. None of these can be confirmed from what is here, and all three artifacts conceded as much in their own records. What I can settle is what each piece is worth, reorder the practical moves on grounds that do not depend on picking a winner, and say what each move would show.

What I am keeping, and on what grounds:

The convergence first. All three artifacts, from incompatible framings, arrive at the same first move: no group settlement meeting; contact the withdrawn flatmate one-to-one with a small ask. When rival diagnoses recommend the same action, the action is better supported than any of the diagnoses, so I adopt it outright.

I accept the objection's central criticism: a fall in recurrence after tightening specifications measures relief, not diagnosis, and the account's test cannot separate the readings. But the remedy is not to drop the probe. It is to pair it with the rival's better observation — how the proposal itself is received. Whether the friend engages with an arrangement's content, pulls back from the very idea of one, or stays silent is more diagnostic than whether the bins stop being argued about. With a caution neither artifact stated: one instance proves little. Pullback is also what overload, a bad week, or distaste for group settings look like. The observation earns weight only across repetitions and only one-to-one, because in a group a person may be declining the audience, not the proposal.

I accept the objection's sequencing complaint but not its implied remedy. The account's order did work the evidence never paid for; that much was right. The answer is not to withhold ordering — a reader with a live problem is owed an order — but to justify the order robustly rather than evidentially: when readings compete and cannot yet be distinguished, prefer the move that is tolerable under the widest range of them. By that test the rival's arrangements (owned zones, default-outcome rotations) move to the front. They are a specification (good if ambiguity is right), they reduce occasions for renegotiation (good under the objection's reading), they reduce exposure (good under the unit-privacy reading), and they reduce tracking load (good under capacity). The account's three-column specification is excellent under one reading and can worsen another, since written done-ness criteria ask more of exactly the person already asking for less. Reversibility, not correctness, is what this material licenses, and every proposal here is cheap to reverse.

I keep the rival's aim — surfacing the unit-privacy axis — and reject its method. Asking a flatmate directly what they take the flat to be will mostly produce puzzlement or a diplomatic answer; stances surface through choices. So the one-to-one contact should offer a concrete choice between two arrangement shapes, sent asynchronously so the reply can come when capacity allows, with 'neither — here's what I'd actually prefer' and 'I don't care' as explicit options. The choice, including the refusal to choose, is the datum the rival wanted from its direct question.

If the answer is silence or 'don't care', the fair default minimizes interaction cost, not work cost. Work expectations stay equal — a zone is still a zone — but negotiation and audit overhead drop to near zero, with zones reassigned by lot at intervals. The lottery has a second virtue none of the artifacts used: it requires nobody to settle whose account of past contributions is right. That matters because of something none of them said. The problem statement is a participant's testimony, not a transcript. 'We disagree about what the agreement meant' is the asker's characterization, and a renegotiation fight — 'you said you'd do the bins' / 'yes, and then my shift changed' — is often remembered afterwards as a meaning fight by whichever side expected the old terms to hold. I am not accusing the asker of distortion; I am declining to treat the description as neutral, which is one more reason to prefer arrangements that do not depend on agreeing about history.

Two revisions rather than adoptions. First, the account's escalation trigger fires on continued avoidance after one or two low-pressure attempts; that conflates refusing conversations with refusing participation. Silent compliance is participation. The trigger should be refusal of arrangements — including refusal by persistent silence across a multi-week window with at least one one-to-one attempt inside it — and the rival's r11 has the right structure with the same flaw, so I take its shape and fix its trigger. When it fires, the living-arrangement question should be named as a question about fit, not levied as a sanction for chore failure. Second, the rival's strict claim that writing specifications enacts one side of a contested question proves too much: audit-light zones enact a stance too, as the rival itself concedes when it worries its reading can shield a flatmate who simply will not do a share. Non-neutrality justifies small, reversible, flagged-as-trial proposals; it does not justify withholding one non-neutral instrument while offering another.

What I keep from the account specifically: the small-item discipline — pilot any arrangement on the two or three chores that actually recur, since the material does not even say which those are — and the fallback column. A pre-declared exit ('if you can't make it, say so the day before') is the piece of the specification move that serves every reading, because it lowers the cost of admitting inability exactly when schedules are unstable.

What stays open: which reading is true; whether the avoidance concerns the household at all; the actual distribution of past work. These are observations only the reader can make, and they will be made by an interested party — that limit should travel with the advice.

The resulting sequence, each step paired with what it would show: (1) a one-to-one, asynchronous offer of two arrangement shapes, 'neither' permitted — the reply's form is the first datum; (2) content-engagement strengthens the ambiguity reading, so tighten done and timing criteria on the recurring items; (3) pullback or silence does not yet establish a household-ontology standoff — set the lottery default with equal work and minimal overhead and ask nothing further; (4) acceptance without discussion is success, not failure, and should not trigger escalation; (5) only if arrangements of every shape are declined or ignored across a real window, name the living-arrangement question explicitly. None of this settles who was right in past arguments, and it is not designed to. Its test is narrower and more honest: whether the household runs with less friction and less conversational overhead while the work stays equal, under whichever reading turns out to be true.","commitments":"{"language":"FCL-1","records":[{"id":"c1","type":"claim","text":"All three artifacts, from incompatible framings, converge on the same first move: no group settlement meeting, and one-to-one, small-ask contact with the withdrawn flatmate. A recommendation that survives rival diagnoses is better supported than any of the diagnoses themselves.","grounds":"The account's step 4, the objection's elevation of the conversational-form reading, and the rival's separate-conversation commitments all arrive at the same action.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c3","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#c1","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r10"]},{"id":"c2","type":"claim","text":"When readings compete and cannot yet be distinguished, the practical ordering should follow robustness and reversibility rather than any evidential ranking of the readings. Audit-light arrangements (owned zones, default-outcome rotations) are tolerable under the ambiguity, renegotiation, unit-privacy, and capacity readings alike, whereas detailed done-ness specifications are high-value mainly under the ambiguity reading and can increase exposure under others.","scope":"Ordering of practical moves given the current undecidability.","consequence":"The rival's arrangement types move ahead of the account's specification move, reversing the account's order on non-evidential grounds.","revises":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2"],"depends":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r8"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o3"]},{"id":"c3","type":"claim","text":"A fall in recurrence after tightening specifications measures relief, not diagnosis; reduced friction on specified items is compatible with every reading in play, so it cannot confirm the ambiguity reading on its own.","grounds":"Accepts the objection's argument that load imbalance or resentment can coexist with reduced friction and that recurrence can resurface as fresh items or after the next schedule change.","depends":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o2"],"revises":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#u1"]},{"id":"c4","type":"claim","text":"How a proposal is received — engagement with its content, pullback from the idea of any arrangement, or silence — carries more diagnostic information than whether disputed items recur, but only cumulatively and in a one-to-one setting, because a single instance is confounded by capacity, mood, and audience.","scope":"The merged probe described in u1.","depends":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r7"]},{"id":"c5","type":"claim","text":"The problem statement is a participant's testimony rather than a neutral transcript: 'we disagree about what the agreement meant' is the asker's characterization, and renegotiation disputes are often remembered afterwards as meaning disputes by whichever side expected the old terms to hold. This implies no bad faith; it implies the description cannot settle the reading.","depends":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o1"]},{"id":"c6","type":"claim","text":"A capacity reading — avoidance reflecting overload from unstable schedules rather than any stance about the household — is consistent with the stated facts, is largely absent from all three artifacts, and is cheap to test by shrinking and asynchronizing the ask.","scope":"Conjecture offered as a fourth reading, not as a diagnosis.","grounds":"The material states schedules change and one friend has begun avoiding the conversations, and contains nothing about the friend's stated reasons, so exhaustion cannot be excluded."},{"id":"c7","type":"claim","text":"If a flatmate declines to co-design arrangements, the fair default minimizes interaction cost rather than work cost: work obligations stay equal while negotiation and audit overhead drop to near zero, with zones reassigned by lot at intervals. Random reassignment also removes the need to settle whose account of past contributions is correct.","grounds":"Declining to co-design is not the same as declining to participate; equal work expectations answer the free-riding worry while removing the conversational overhead the withdrawn flatmate may be avoiding.","depends":["c5","c6"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r9","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r8"]},{"id":"o1","type":"objection","text":"The rival's method for surfacing the unit-privacy axis — asking flatmates directly what they take the flat to be — will tend to produce puzzled or strategic answers rather than reliable stances.","bearing":"The aim of r6 survives; the method should be replaced by choices between concrete arrangements, whose selection (including refusal to choose) reveals the stance.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r6"]},{"id":"o2","type":"objection","text":"The rival's non-neutrality point proves too much in its strict form: audit-light zones also enact a stance about the household, as the rival itself concedes when it worries its reading can shield a flatmate unwilling to do a share.","bearing":"Non-neutrality justifies proposals that are small, reversible, and flagged as trials; it does not justify withholding specification while offering alternatives, since the alternatives are equally non-neutral.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r3"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r9"]},{"id":"o3","type":"objection","text":"The objection's complaint about construction from thin material is only half right: the defect was not that the account constructed much, but that its ordering presented pragmatic choices as though evidentially ranked. The remedy is explicit robustness and trigger grounds, not refusal to order — a reader with a live problem is owed an order, provided its justifications are visible.","bearing":"If ordering is withheld whenever material is thin, tentativeness becomes unusable; conditionality preserves tentativeness while keeping the advice actionable.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o3"]},{"id":"o4","type":"objection","text":"My own reception-observation (c4) is weak evidence in any single instance and is read by an interested party hoping for a particular answer; pullback from a proposal is over-determined (privacy stance, capacity, fatigue, mood, audience).","bearing":"c4's observation should never by itself trigger the escalation in k3, and the asker's reading of the friend's replies should be treated as fallible.","target":["c4"]},{"id":"u1","type":"use","text":"Open with the merged first move: a one-to-one, asynchronous message to the withdrawn flatmate offering a choice between two arrangement shapes — audit-light owned zones with periodic reassignment by lot, or a shared rotation with default timing — with 'neither, here's what I'd actually prefer' and 'I don't care' as explicit options.","action":"Send as a message rather than a scheduled talk, so the reply can come when capacity allows; frame both shapes as trials that can be changed.","consequence":"One low-cost move delivers the account's step 4, the surface the rival wanted from r6, the observation the rival wanted from r7, and the capacity test in c6 simultaneously.","depends":["c1","c4","c6","o1"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c3","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r7","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r8"]},{"id":"u2","type":"use","text":"If the reply is silence or 'don't care', set the default per c7 without treating the non-reply as a stance: run the lottery with equal work obligations and near-zero audit, and say once, without reproach, that it can be changed on request.","depends":["c7"],"consequence":"The household runs whether or not the withdrawn flatmate ever re-enters conversation; no further asks are made until the window in k3 closes."},{"id":"u3","type":"use","text":"Retain from the account the fallback column: a pre-declared exit ('if you can't do it by the agreed time, say so the day before') attached to whatever arrangement is adopted.","grounds":"Pre-declared exits lower the cost of admitting inability exactly when schedules are unstable, which serves the ambiguity, renegotiation, and capacity readings alike.","depends":["c6"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2"]},{"id":"u4","type":"use","text":"Keep the account's small-item discipline: pilot any arrangement on the two or three chores that actually recur rather than codifying the whole household.","action":"List the recurring items first; anything not on the list stays informal.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#p1"]},{"id":"k1","type":"commitment","text":"If the withdrawn flatmate engages with the content of either arrangement shape, treat the ambiguity reading as strengthened and proceed to tighten done and timing criteria on the two or three recurring items.","scope":"Contingent on the reply's form as described in c4.","action":"Move from the trial arrangement to explicit done/timing/fallback columns on the recurring items only.","consequence":"The account's specification move is retained as a second-stage response to evidence, not as the opening default.","depends":["c4","c3"]},{"id":"k2","type":"commitment","text":"If the flatmate accepts an audit-light arrangement but declines discussion, treat that as participation and success: do not escalate, do not press for conversation, and keep interaction overhead minimal.","grounds":"Silent compliance is participation; the account's step-5 trigger conflates refusing conversations with refusing participation.","depends":["c7","o4"]},{"id":"k3","type":"commitment","text":"Escalate to the living-arrangement question only when arrangements of every offered shape are declined or ignored across a multi-week window that includes at least one one-to-one attempt; 'one or two attempts' is too small a basis for a decision the size of the lease.","depends":["c4","k2","o4"],"revises":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r11"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#o1"]},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"Which reading holds — ambiguity, renegotiation or legitimacy, unit-versus-privacy, or capacity — cannot be determined from the material, and the discriminating observations will be made by an interested party. Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node response

Continue the inquiry in light of the account, criticism and alternative. Decide what to use, leave open, revise or reject, and explain your grounds where they matter.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account

Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: cd6e3e2f307e0dac79543de9bed087db4ee7dcd40b3d989d3c6d4b02057d8b99
Original body SHA256: 360ee14fa7545c90cadf79c7d2fe9c157faf470d6368504b06768e36e0d13c79
Original commitments SHA256: bd7faa10242d5841c8063c7a0919a20706c658c4a2054a5729caeacbc3cd04c8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The problem as posed is practical, and the material is thin: three flatmates, recurring disputes about ordinary chores, agreements that later turn out to have been understood differently, changing work schedules, and one friend withdrawing from the conversation. There is also a first-fork note saying the prior source was absent in the first template invocation, so there is no earlier account to inherit or revise against. I should not pretend to know what was said in prior conversations, what the chores are, who is avoiding whom, or why.

The most useful thing to conjecture is that the repeated disagreement is not primarily about willingness. Two people can agree that the dishes should be done and still disagree later about whether the agreement meant "by tonight," "before the kitchen is used again," or "on your turn." That is an ambiguity problem, not a motivation problem. Changing schedules make any fixed arrangement fragile, and avoidance is a predictable response when each conversation feels like relitigating fault. So the working hypothesis is: the household is running on spoken agreements with unstated specifications, and the cost of that ambiguity has become high enough that one participant is exiting the conversation rather than re-entering it.

A second, less certain hypothesis is that the avoidance is about the form of the conversations rather than the chores. If past talks ended in grievance or in one person doing most of the negotiating work, withdrawal is a sensible local strategy. I cannot tell from the material whether that is happening.

What I would try, roughly in order:

1. Separate the recurring disputes into the smallest repeated cases (e.g. kitchen surfaces, bins, bathroom, shared shopping). Do not start with a general talk about fairness; start with two or three concrete items that actually recur.

2. For each item, write down three things in a shared note: what counts as done, when it counts as done, and what happens when someone cannot do it. The third column matters because schedules change. "If you cannot do it by the agreed time, say so the day before and the other two decide" is different from "whoever notices does it."

3. Treat the written note as a draft, not a contract. Its purpose is to surface disagreement while it is still about a chore rather than about a person. If a written version feels too formal, a shared message thread or a note on the fridge does the same work with less ceremony.

4. Approach the friend who is avoiding the conversations separately and with a smaller ask. Not "we need to talk about the house," which invites the same argument, but "I noticed you've been quiet about this; I'd rather not keep pushing it in the group. Can we spend ten minutes on just the bins and the kitchen?" Give that person an easier entry point, and accept a lower-commitment role at first.

5. If the avoidance continues after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop treating it as a scheduling problem. Then the question becomes whether the living arrangement itself still works. That is a larger decision and should not be forced by a chore dispute, but it should not be indefinitely deferred either.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting intended to settle everything, moral language about "pulling weight," and counting instances as evidence in the moment. Those tend to convert a specification problem into a character dispute, which is exactly the shape the current disagreement already has.

I should be clear about what this is not. It is not a claim that the withdrawing friend is acting in good faith; I do not know. It is not a claim that the others are blameless. It is not a claim that written agreements work for every household. It is a conjecture that a large share of the recurring friction is ambiguity under shifting schedules, and that the ambiguity is addressable independently of who is right about any particular past disagreement. The strongest test of that conjecture is whether two or three concrete items, specified more tightly, stop recurring. If they do not, the hypothesis is wrong and the problem is probably about the relationship or the living arrangement rather than the chores.
COMMITMENTS

The avoidance could be about conflict fatigue, unequal load, or something outside the chores entirely, and formalizing chores could make things worse rather than better.","bearing":"If load imbalance or relational conflict is the real driver, the specification move in c2 may treat a symptom, and step 5 arrives too late."},{"id":"u1","type":"use","text":"Ask the reader to test c2 on two or three concrete recurring chores before adopting step 5, and to report whether recurrence falls.","action":"Read the account as a working hypothesis to try in the next week or two, not as an endorsed plan."},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"The material does not say what the recurring chores are, how long this has gone on, or whether the withdrawing friend has said anything about why. Without that, all of the above stays at the level of a plausible but untested hypothesis.","mentions":["c1","c2","c3"]}],"uptake":["c1","c2","c3","o1","u1"]}

## Selected input objection

Source objection: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection; selected view: both
Artifact: 406eff787391049a53c08a1fa638c1576c4a54c65be4bdde122593deb25fdbbe
Original body SHA256: 6dbebbfd0f40783c19873f2a045833055ecb090fecd9801cf39854f6f527ec0b
Original commitments SHA256: 9ffd96b23205ac092c5306bf372afa156fbb5159a3a259197c9ace200a835dc1
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
I want to push on the account's central move: recasting the conflict as a problem of specification rather than a problem of motivation or fairness. That recasting is doing a great deal of work, and the material does not obviously support it.

Look at what the statement of the problem actually reports. Three people sharing a flat quarrel over routine chores. On occasion they agree who will do a task, and afterwards fall out over what the agreement meant. Timetables shift. One person has begun to steer clear of the conversations. The recurring "later disagreement about what it meant" is read by the account as evidence that the agreements were ambiguous. Yet the same observation is equally consistent with an alternative reading: the agreement was clear enough, and the later dispute is about whether the terms still bind given changed circumstances, or about who has standing to enforce them. "You said you'd do the bins" / "yes, and then my shift changed" is not necessarily a problem of semantics. It can be a problem of renegotiation, or one of legitimacy.

In o1 the account acknowledges this, yet it then treats the ambiguity hypothesis as the working one and gives less weight to the alternatives. That is a defensible starting point if one has to be chosen, but the diagnostic step the account itself proposes - try two or three concrete items and see if recurrence falls - is weaker than it looks, since a specification move can lower friction while the driver underneath is load imbalance or resentment. Tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement are still a lopsided arrangement, only with clearer paperwork. A fall in recurrence would be consistent with the ambiguity hypothesis, but the rival hypotheses forecast a different pattern: recurrence might fall on the items specified and resurface as fresh complaint items, or fall for a time and then come back at the next change of circumstances. These are not told apart by the account's test.

There is also an issue of phrasing worth flagging. The account states that the problem as posed is "practical" and the material is "thin." Those are the author's characterizations, not features of the situation. As a caution, calling the material thin is fine, but the thinness is then used by the account to license a good deal of construction (the three-column spec, the low-pressure approach to the withdrawing friend, the step-5 threshold). Thin material supports tentative proposals; it does not support ordering those proposals as if the ambiguity reading had already earned its place at the front.

Probably the most useful move in the account is the one it treats as secondary: that the avoidance may concern the form of the conversations rather than the chores. That deserves to be nearer the front, since it is the part of the situation that is genuinely distinctive and that the specific-negotiation advice does not address. A tight spec on bins does not bring a withdrawn flatmate back into the room. At c3 and step 4 the account half-sees this, yet the overall frame still centers the chores.

What I would not assert: that the ambiguity hypothesis is mistaken. I cannot judge from the material. My objection is to the ordering and to the strength of the test, not to the plausibility of the hypothesis. If the account were rewritten with the conversational-form reading as the first hypothesis and the spec move as one probe among several, I would have less to say against it.
COMMITMENTS

BODY
The rival framing I want to try is not another chore protocol. It is the question of what the agreements were for.

The selected account treats the trouble as ambiguity in specifications: agreements lack criteria for done-ness and timing, schedules shift, so friction recurs. That is a good hypothesis as far as it goes, and I have no material that contradicts it. But it quietly assumes that everyone wanted a specification. The avoidance suggests the opposite for at least one flatmate. A person can stay away from a conversation not because the terms are vague but because any settled term would feel like a binding owed to people they live with, and that is a different problem from the one the selected account addresses.

So the rival pose is: maybe the disputes are not failing negotiations about tasks. Maybe they are negotiations about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. Under that reading, writing down "what counts as done" is not neutral — it is one side of a contested question, enacted without having settled it. Shifting schedules are then not merely a complication; they are the fact that makes the unit-reading feel coercive to the person who is withdrawing.

I cannot tell which reading is right from the material. What I can do is name a test that distinguishes them rather than assuming one. The selected account's test is whether tightened specifications stop recurrences. Mine adds a second: when specifications are proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with their content or pull back from the proposal itself? Content-engagement supports the ambiguity reading. Pullback from the very idea of a written arrangement supports the unit-versus-privacy reading.

Roughly what I would do differently from the selected account:

1. Do not open with a shared note. Open by asking the two flatmates, separately, what they think the flat is — a shared project with mutual obligations, or three lives that happen to overlap in a kitchen. Do not ask it as a survey; ask it as a real disagreement I am willing to hear out.

2. If the answers diverge, treat that as the actual dispute, and treat the chores as the surface where it keeps surfacing. Chore rules can then be framed as a truce between two readings rather than as a correct specification that one side has been failing to meet.

3. Consider an arrangement that does not require agreement on meaning: individually-owned zones, or a rotation with a default outcome that nobody has to negotiate in the moment (for example, each person is responsible for a defined zone and the group does not audit it). This trades efficiency for reduced exposure, which is what a privacy-reading flatmate may actually want.

4. If one or both flatmates reject even truce-shaped arrangements, stop optimizing chores and start asking whether the lease and living arrangement still fit. That is not a chore failure.

What I am not claiming: that the withdrawing flatmate is the reasonable one, that written rules are coercive in general, or that the ambiguity reading is wrong. The selected account's diagnosis may well be correct and mine may simply add a second axis. The point of the rival is to make the second axis visible, because a plan that only addresses ambiguity will keep running into a wall if the disagreement is about what kind of household this is.
